To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the standard of care (oral ampicillin) is better than the comparator drug (oral cefixime), that the difference is small, and that the standard of oral ampicillin can be safely used in children aged 2 months to 5 years with chest indrawing pneumonia, even when the child is not very sick.

“In settings with limited access to inpatient facilities, treatment of children with pneumonia who have chest indrawing but are not toxic (ie, no danger signs) with oral ampicillin plus gentamicin is superior to oral amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav alone, and is not associated with a signifi cantly higher risk of adverse events.”

(1) in the context of a low-resource setting, antibiotics are effective in reducing mortality in children with severe pneumonia; (2) the use of antibiotics in children with pneumonia and chest indrawing but not danger signs is associated with a low mortality; and (3) the use of oral antibiotics in the outpatient management of children with pneumonia and no danger signs is associated also with a low mortality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a practical approach to treat children in outpatient settings in resource-poor settings, in which the vast majority of children with pneumonia are treated.
the treatment of children who cannot access inpatient care.
the question of what to do in a setting in which the only available treatment is oral antibiotics.

there are no valid studies to guide treatment of children with pneumonia in resource-limited settings, and therefore no basis for any recommendation.
the evidence for the WHO policy of treating all children with pneumonia with a broad-spectrum antibiotic is weak, and more research is needed.

the WHO guidelines for the management of childhood pneumonia are evidence based and that the studies used in the guidelines were done in a variety of countries, and that these guidelines are the best evidence currently available.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that in the outpatient setting in which the vast majority of babies with pneumonia live, oral antibiotics can be used safely and effectively.
the trials we did were done with the best methods possible, given the constraints of the settings in which the studies were done.

, in the context of the limitations of the WHO diagnostic criteria and the lack of microbiological facilities, we believe that oral antibiotics (ie, amoxicillin) should be used to treat children with chest indrawing, with or without fever, in outpatient settings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can save the lives of babies and young children with pneumonia by providing them with the right antibiotic treatment in the right setting, and that the best setting is in the home.
we can treat babies with antibiotics in the clinic or in the community with a reasonable chance of preventing death.
, although we cannot distinguish bacterial and viral pneumonia, the WHO guidelines for treatment of pneumonia are based on the best available evidence and have been shown to be lifesaving.
